title: How Many Drinks in a Bottle of Wine? Glasses, Units, and ABV Math
excerpt: A 750 mL bottle of wine holds about 5 standard drinks at 12%, and closer to 6 for most reds. Glasses, UK units, Australian drinks, and a ten-second formula for any bottle.
metaDescription: A bottle of wine holds about 5 standard drinks at 12% ABV and nearly 6 for most reds. See glasses per bottle, UK units, and a quick formula for any wine.
author: DHM Guide Team
tags: how many drinks in a bottle of wine
content:
**The short answer:** a standard 750 mL bottle of wine at 12% alcohol holds about **5 standard drinks** by US measurements. Most wine on the shelf today is stronger than that, though. A typical 13.5% red holds closer to **5.7 drinks**, and a big 15% Zinfandel or Amarone holds more than **6**. In glasses, that same bottle pours five 5-ounce glasses, four 6-ounce restaurant pours, or only about three of the large, generous glasses many of us pour at home.

If you're in the UK, a 750 mL bottle at 13.5% is about **10 units**, which is most of the 14-unit weekly guideline in a single bottle. In Australia, the same bottle is about **8 standard drinks**, and Australian labels are required to print the exact number.

This guide shows you how to work out the number for any bottle in about ten seconds, explains why "a glass of wine" is a much less precise measure than it sounds, and covers what a bottle actually means for your evening, your sleep, and your next morning.

## How Many Standard Drinks Are in a Bottle of Wine?

A "standard drink" isn't a glass. It's a fixed amount of pure alcohol. In the US, the National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism (NIAAA) defines one standard drink as **14 grams of pure alcohol**, which is about 0.6 fluid ounces. That's roughly the amount in:

- 12 oz of regular beer at about 5% alcohol
- 5 oz of wine at about 12% alcohol
- 1.5 oz of 80-proof spirits (40% alcohol)

A standard bottle of wine is 750 mL, or about 25.4 fluid ounces. If the wine is exactly 12% alcohol by volume (ABV), the bottle contains about 90 mL of pure alcohol, which weighs about 71 grams. Divide 71 by 14 and you get just over 5. That's where the familiar "five glasses in a bottle" comes from.

The problem is that 12% is the low end for a lot of modern wine. Here's how the count changes with the ABV printed on the label:

| Wine strength (ABV) | Typical examples | US standard drinks per 750 mL bottle |
|---|---|---|
| 5.5% | Moscato d'Asti | about 2.3 |
| 9% | German Riesling Kabinett | about 3.8 |
| 11% | Prosecco, Vinho Verde, lighter whites | about 4.6 |
| 12% | Champagne, many Pinot Grigios | about 5.1 |
| 13% | Sauvignon Blanc, many Pinot Noirs | about 5.5 |
| 13.5% | Merlot, Malbec, Rioja, many Chardonnays | about 5.7 |
| 14.5% | California Cabernet, Shiraz, Grenache | about 6.1 |
| 15% | Zinfandel, Amarone | about 6.3 |
| 20% | Port (fortified) | about 8.5 |

The gap between the lightest and strongest table wines is bigger than most people expect. A bottle of 14.5% Cabernet carries roughly 20% more alcohol than a bottle of 12% Pinot Grigio, even though both bottles look identical on the table.

### The ten-second formula

You can work out the standard drinks in any bottle with one simple calculation:

**Standard drinks = bottle size in mL × ABV ÷ 1,774**

For a 750 mL bottle you can shorten it even more: **multiply the ABV by 0.42.** So a 13.5% bottle is 13.5 × 0.42 = about 5.7 drinks, and a 14% bottle is about 5.9.

If that's still too much math at a dinner party, use this rule of thumb: **a bottle of wine is about five drinks at 12%, and adds roughly one more drink for every 2.5 points of ABV above that.**

### Label ABV is an estimate, not a guarantee

The number on the label isn't always exact. In the US, the Alcohol and Tobacco Tax and Trade Bureau (TTB) allows wine labeled at 14% ABV or less to be off by up to 1.5 percentage points, and wine above 14% to be off by up to 1 point. A wine labeled 13.5% could legally be 15%. Wine writers and lab tests have repeatedly found that many wines run a little stronger than the label says, so if anything, the numbers above are more likely to be a slight undercount than an overcount.

## How Many Glasses of Wine Are in a Bottle?

This is where the numbers get slippery, because a "glass" depends entirely on who's pouring and into what.

| Pour size | Glasses per 750 mL bottle | Standard drinks per glass (at 13.5%) |
|---|---|---|
| 4 oz (about 120 mL), a tasting or light pour | about 6 | about 0.9 |
| 5 oz (about 150 mL), the "official" glass | 5 | about 1.1 |
| 6 oz (about 175 mL), a common restaurant pour | about 4 | about 1.4 |
| 8 oz (about 240 mL), a generous home pour | about 3 | about 1.8 |
| 9 oz (250 mL), a UK "large" glass | 3 | about 1.9 |

Two things stand out. First, the 5-ounce "standard" glass is smaller than most people think. Pour 5 oz into a modern wine glass and it often looks like barely a third full. Second, the alcohol in a glass depends on both the pour and the wine. An 8-ounce pour of 14.5% Cabernet is close to **two** standard drinks in one glass.

### Why your glass is bigger than you think

Wine glasses have grown a lot over time. A 2017 study in The BMJ looked at English wine glasses going back to the 1700s and found their average capacity had grown roughly sevenfold, with the steepest increase in recent decades. Researchers at the University of Cambridge have also found that serving wine in larger glasses was linked to more wine being sold in some bars and restaurants, even when the pour size stayed the same.

The practical upshot: if you pour at home by eye, especially into a large-bowled glass, your "one glass" is probably more than 5 ounces. If you want to know what a real 5-ounce pour looks like, measure it once with a measuring cup and notice where it sits in your usual glass. It's an eye-opener for most people, and it takes 30 seconds.

### Restaurant pours

Many US restaurants pour 5 to 6 ounces by the glass, and some pour more. In the UK, wine by the glass is commonly sold in 125 mL, 175 mL, and 250 mL sizes. A 250 mL "large" glass is exactly one-third of a bottle. Order two large glasses over dinner and you've had two-thirds of a bottle, which is about 6.7 UK units at 13.5%.

## How Many Units Are in a Bottle of Wine? (UK)

The UK uses "units" instead of standard drinks. One UK unit is **10 mL (8 grams) of pure alcohol**, which is smaller than a US standard drink. That's why the UK numbers look bigger.

The UK formula is simple: **units = ABV × volume in litres.** For a 750 mL bottle, that's ABV × 0.75.

| ABV | UK units per 750 mL bottle |
|---|---|
| 11% | about 8.3 |
| 12% | 9 |
| 13% | about 9.8 |
| 13.5% | about 10.1 |
| 14% | 10.5 |
| 15% | about 11.3 |

The UK Chief Medical Officers' guideline is to drink no more than **14 units a week** on a regular basis, spread over three or more days. A single bottle of 13.5% wine is about 10 units. So a bottle and a half of a typical red across the whole week is roughly the guideline limit, and one bottle shared between two people is about 5 units each.

By the glass:

- A small 125 mL glass of 13% wine is about 1.6 units.
- A standard 175 mL glass of 13% wine is about 2.3 units.
- A large 250 mL glass of 13% wine is about 3.3 units.

## How Many Standard Drinks Are in a Bottle of Wine in Australia and Canada?

Countries don't agree on how big a "drink" is, which is one reason numbers online seem to contradict each other.

**Australia** defines a standard drink as **10 grams of alcohol**. A 750 mL bottle at 13% contains about 7.7 standard drinks, and a 14.5% red is about 8.6. Australian law requires alcohol labels to state the number of standard drinks, so you can simply check the back of the bottle. Australia's national guidelines, from the National Health and Medical Research Council, advise healthy adults to drink no more than 10 standard drinks a week and no more than 4 on any one day. A single bottle of red is already more than the daily figure.

**Canada** defines a standard drink as about **13.45 grams of alcohol**, which is close to the US measure. A 750 mL bottle at 13% works out to roughly 5.7 Canadian standard drinks. Canada's 2023 Guidance on Alcohol and Health takes a more cautious line than older advice and describes health risk as rising steadily with each additional drink per week.

**The US** uses 14 grams. The US Dietary Guidelines for Americans have long advised that adults who drink should limit themselves to 2 drinks or fewer a day for men and 1 drink or fewer a day for women.

The bottle doesn't change from country to country. Only the size of the measuring cup does.

## Other Bottle Sizes: Half Bottles, Magnums, Boxes, and Cans

Not all wine comes in 750 mL bottles. Here's what other common formats hold, assuming a 13% wine:

| Format | Volume | Equivalent in standard bottles | US standard drinks (at 13%) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Single-serve can (small) | 250 mL | one-third | about 1.8 |
| Mini bottle or "split" | 187.5 mL | one-quarter | about 1.4 |
| Single-serve can (large) | 375 mL | one-half | about 2.7 |
| Half bottle | 375 mL | one-half | about 2.7 |
| Standard bottle | 750 mL | 1 | about 5.5 |
| Magnum | 1.5 L | 2 | about 11 |
| Box wine | 3 L | 4 | about 22 |

Cans deserve a special note. A 375 mL can of wine looks like a can of soda, but it holds half a bottle, which is close to three standard drinks. People often treat a can as "one drink," and it's really closer to three.

Box wine has the opposite problem. Because there's no visible level dropping in a bottle, it's very easy to lose track. A 3-liter box holds the same wine as four bottles, so if a box disappears over a week, that's four bottles' worth.

## How Many Shots Are in a Bottle of Wine?

People sometimes ask this to compare wine with spirits. By volume, a 750 mL bottle holds about 17 shot glasses (1.5 oz each). But that comparison is misleading, because a shot of liquor is about 40% alcohol and wine is about 12 to 15%.

The fairer comparison is by alcohol content. **A bottle of 12% wine contains about the same amount of alcohol as five shots of 80-proof vodka or whiskey.** A 14.5% red is closer to six shots. Drinking a bottle of wine over dinner puts roughly the same amount of alcohol into your body as taking five or six shots, just more slowly.

That "more slowly" matters. Sipping over two or three hours with food gives your body more time to process the alcohol, so your peak blood alcohol is lower than if you took the same amount quickly. But the total amount of alcohol your liver has to handle is the same.

## How Much Alcohol Is in a Bottle of Wine (in Grams and Calories)?

At 12% ABV, a 750 mL bottle contains about **71 grams of pure alcohol**. At 13.5%, it's about **80 grams**, and at 15%, about **89 grams**.

Alcohol provides about 7 calories per gram, so the alcohol alone in a 13.5% bottle supplies roughly 560 calories. A typical dry red or white bottle lands somewhere around 600 to 650 calories in total, and sweeter or higher-alcohol wines can be more. For comparison, that's similar to a large restaurant main course, which is worth knowing if you're tracking your weight.

## Is a Bottle of Wine a Day Too Much?

For most people, yes. It helps to compare a bottle with the commonly used guideline limits:

- **US:** a bottle at 13.5% is about 5.7 standard drinks. The NIAAA describes heavy drinking as more than 4 drinks on any day or more than 14 a week for men, and more than 3 on any day or more than 7 a week for women. A bottle a day is about 40 drinks a week.
- **UK:** a bottle a day at 13.5% is about 70 units a week, five times the 14-unit guideline.
- **Australia:** a bottle a day is about 56 standard drinks a week, more than five times the 10-drink guideline.

A bottle a day is a heavy, regular intake by any of these definitions, and it's associated with higher risks for liver disease, high blood pressure, heart rhythm problems, several cancers (including breast and bowel cancer), poor sleep, and weight gain. Wine isn't a special case here. Your body handles the alcohol in wine the same way it handles the alcohol in beer or spirits.

What about the idea that red wine is good for your heart? That belief comes largely from older observational studies and from interest in resveratrol, a compound in grape skins. Newer research has been much more skeptical. The amount of resveratrol in wine is small, and studies that account for factors like overall health, income, and diet have weakened the case that moderate drinking protects the heart. There's no good evidence that drinking wine is a healthy choice for someone who doesn't already drink.

### What about half a bottle?

Half a bottle of 13.5% wine is nearly 3 US standard drinks, or about 5 UK units. For many women in particular, that's already above common single-day guidelines. Split a bottle with a partner every night, and each person is drinking around 20 US standard drinks, or 35 UK units, a week.

If you've drifted into a nightly bottle or half-bottle habit and want to cut back, a few practical steps help: buy smaller formats like half bottles, choose lower-alcohol wines (11 to 12.5% instead of 14.5%), measure a real 5-ounce pour, and set a few alcohol-free nights each week. If you've been drinking a bottle or more every day for a while, talk to your doctor before stopping suddenly (see the box below).

## How Many Glasses of Wine to Get Drunk?

There's no single answer, because it depends on your body size, sex, whether you've eaten, how fast you drink, and the strength of the wine. A few general points hold up well:

- **Most adults feel noticeable effects after about 2 standard drinks**, which is two 5-ounce glasses, or often just one and a half generous home pours.
- **Women generally reach a higher blood alcohol level than men** from the same amount of wine, mostly because of differences in body size and body water.
- **An empty stomach speeds things up.** Alcohol absorbs much faster when your stomach is empty, so the same two glasses hit harder before dinner than with dinner. Our guide to [drinking on an empty stomach](/never-hungover/drinking-on-an-empty-stomach) explains why.
- **Your body clears roughly one standard drink per hour on average**, though it varies from person to person. Nothing reliably speeds that up much, as we explain in [how to speed up alcohol metabolism](/never-hungover/how-to-speed-up-alcohol-metabolism).

For a rough sense of scale, the NIAAA defines binge drinking as a pattern that brings blood alcohol to 0.08% or above, which typically happens when women have about 4 drinks or men have about 5 drinks within about 2 hours. A single bottle of 13.5% wine shared by two people over a long dinner usually stays below that. One person finishing a bottle in two hours is over it.

**Never drive after drinking wine based on a glass count.** Pour sizes and wine strength vary too much to guess your blood alcohol level reliably. If you've been drinking, don't drive.

> **When to get help, and when to talk to a doctor.** This article is general information, not medical advice.
>
> **Call 911 (or your local emergency number) right away** if someone who has been drinking is confused or hard to wake, is vomiting while drowsy, has slow or irregular breathing (fewer than 8 breaths a minute or long pauses), has a seizure, or has pale, bluish, or cold skin. These are signs of alcohol poisoning. Don't leave them to "sleep it off." Keep them on their side and stay with them until help arrives.
>
> **Talk to your doctor** if you regularly drink a bottle or more a day, if you find it hard to stick to the amount you planned, or if you take medicines that interact with alcohol. If you've been drinking heavily every day, don't stop all at once without advice. Shakiness, sweating, a racing heart, anxiety, or trouble sleeping when you go without a drink can be signs of alcohol withdrawal, which can become serious and is safest managed with a doctor's help.

## Does a Bottle of Wine Cause a Worse Hangover Than Other Drinks?

The biggest driver of how bad you feel the next morning is how much alcohol you had in total, not what kind. A bottle of 14.5% red is about six standard drinks, and six drinks of anything is likely to leave a mark.

That said, a few things make wine hangovers feel distinctive:

- **It's easy to underestimate the amount.** Refills, big glasses, and strong wines mean people often drink more than they think.
- **Red wine is high in congeners**, the by-products of fermentation and aging that give dark drinks their flavor. Darker drinks with more congeners have been linked to worse hangovers in studies comparing bourbon and vodka, and the same idea is often applied to red wine.
- **Some people get headaches from red wine specifically**, sometimes after only a glass. We break down the possible causes, including flavanols like quercetin, histamine, and tannins, in our guide to [red wine headaches](/never-hungover/red-wine-headache).
- **Sulfites get blamed but are usually not the cause.** White wine typically contains more sulfites than red, and many dried fruits contain far more than either. Our article on [sulfites in wine and headaches](/never-hungover/sulfites-in-wine-headaches) covers who actually reacts to them.
- **Sweet and sparkling wines** can go to your head faster. Bubbles may speed alcohol absorption, and sweetness makes it easier to drink quickly.

For a full walkthrough of why wine hangovers happen and what helps, see our [wine hangover guide](/never-hungover/wine-hangover-guide).

## Practical Ways to Keep Track of Wine

Knowing that a bottle holds five or six drinks is useful only if you can apply it in the moment. These habits make it easier:

1. **Check the ABV before you open the bottle.** It's usually on the front or back label. Use the shortcut: ABV × 0.42 = US standard drinks in the bottle.
2. **Measure one pour at home.** Pour 5 oz (150 mL) into your usual glass once, and remember where it sits.
3. **Use smaller glasses.** It's an easy way to slow down without feeling deprived.
4. **Don't top up a half-full glass.** Constant refills make it nearly impossible to count. Finish a glass before pouring another.
5. **Alternate with water.** A glass of water between glasses of wine slows your pace and helps with thirst the next day.
6. **Eat with your wine.** Food slows how quickly alcohol is absorbed and keeps your peak blood alcohol lower.
7. **Pick lighter wines on big nights.** Choosing a 12% white over a 14.5% red means about 20% less alcohol per bottle, with no change in how many glasses you pour.
8. **Buy the size you mean to drink.** A half bottle or a 250 mL can makes stopping easy.

## A Word on Supplements

If you're planning a dinner where a bottle will be shared, the most reliable ways to feel better the next day are still the basics: drink less, drink slower, eat, and keep water on the table. No supplement changes the number of drinks in a bottle or makes heavy drinking safe.

Some people also take dihydromyricetin (DHM), a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree, before or while drinking. Early research, mostly in animals, suggests DHM may support how the body processes alcohol and its by-products, but human evidence is limited, and there is no good evidence that it prevents hangovers outright. If you'd like to try it, popular options include [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20) and [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers timing and amounts, and [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits that matter more.

## The Bottom Line

A 750 mL bottle of wine holds about **5 US standard drinks at 12% ABV**, and closer to **6 for the 13.5 to 15% wines** that fill most shelves. That's about **9 to 11 UK units** or **7 to 9 Australian standard drinks**. In glasses, it's five 5-ounce pours, four restaurant pours, or three generous home pours.

To get the real number for any bottle, multiply the ABV by 0.42 for US drinks, or by 0.75 for UK units. Measure a real pour once, keep an eye on the ABV, and remember that a "glass" of wine is often more than one drink.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**How many standard drinks are in a 750 mL bottle of wine?**

About 5 at 12% ABV, using the US definition of a standard drink (14 grams of alcohol). Most modern wines are stronger, so a 13.5% bottle holds about 5.7 and a 15% bottle about 6.3. To check any bottle, multiply the ABV on the label by 0.42.

**How many glasses of wine are in a bottle?**

A 750 mL bottle pours five 5-ounce glasses, about four 6-ounce restaurant glasses, or about three 8-ounce home pours. In the UK, it's six 125 mL glasses, about four 175 mL glasses, or three 250 mL large glasses.

**How many units are in a bottle of wine?**

Multiply the ABV by 0.75. A bottle at 12% is 9 UK units, at 13.5% about 10 units, and at 14.5% about 11 units. The UK guideline is no more than 14 units a week, so one bottle of a typical red is most of a week's limit.

**Is a bottle of wine a day too much?**

Yes, by every major guideline. A bottle a day is about 40 US standard drinks or 70 UK units a week, well above heavy-drinking thresholds, and is linked to higher risks of liver disease, high blood pressure, several cancers, and poor sleep. If you drink this much regularly, talk to your doctor, and don't stop suddenly without advice if you've been drinking heavily every day.

**Is a glass of wine one drink?**

Only if it's a 5-ounce pour of wine at about 12%. Many glasses are bigger and many wines are stronger. An 8-ounce pour of 14.5% red is close to two standard drinks.

**How many shots are in a bottle of wine?**

By volume, a 750 mL bottle holds about 17 1.5-ounce shots, but that's not a fair comparison. By alcohol content, a bottle of 12% wine equals about five shots of 80-proof liquor, and a 14.5% red is about six.

**How many drinks are in a bottle of wine in Australia?**

Australia uses a 10-gram standard drink, so a 750 mL bottle at 13% contains about 7.7 standard drinks and a 14.5% red about 8.6. Australian labels must state the exact number, so check the back of the bottle.

**How many drinks are in a box of wine?**

A standard 3-liter box holds the same as four 750 mL bottles. At 13%, that's about 22 US standard drinks, or about 20 at 12%.

**How long does it take to process a bottle of wine?**

The body clears roughly one standard drink per hour on average, so a bottle of 13.5% wine, at about 5.7 drinks, takes around five to six hours to clear after you stop drinking, and longer for some people. Coffee, cold showers, and exercise don't meaningfully speed this up. If you've had a bottle in the evening, you may still have alcohol in your system the next morning.
